content: Flunixin is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that also possesses analgesic and antipyretic properties. It is commonly used in horses, cattle, and pigs. The drug is often formulated as its meglumine salt. In the United States, its distribution is regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and requires a prescription from a licensed veterinarian. Flunixin is marketed under various trade names, which are listed below. The full analgesic and antipyretic effects of flunixin typically manifest within 1 to 2 hours after administration. However, an effective analgesic response can often be observed as early as 15 minutes post-treatment. The drug's effects can last for up to 30 hours, with peak efficacy occurring between 2 and 16 hours after administration. This prolonged effect is likely due to the drug's accumulation at sites of inflammation. Flunixin is primarily used to manage colic pain, muscle pain, joint disease, and to reduce fevers and pain. It is also effective in preventing endotoxemia and treating eye injuries. Flunixin should not be administered for more than five consecutive days. Like other NSAIDs, it can cause gastrointestinal (GI) side effects, particularly when given in high doses or over extended periods. The most common adverse effect is GI ulceration, which frequently occurs in the large colon or stomach of the animal. Prolonged use increases the risk of this complication. Other potential side effects include kidney damage and bleeding disorders. Flunixin should be used cautiously in horses with pre-existing kidney or liver disease. It is important to note that flunixin does not address the underlying cause of fever or pain but only alleviates the symptoms. Additionally, pain can serve as a diagnostic tool for veterinarians, and masking it with flunixin may hinder accurate diagnosis. For this reason, some veterinarians prefer to withhold flunixin in cases of suspected colic until the need for surgical intervention has been determined. It is advisable to consult the horse's veterinarian before administering the drug. Flunixin is classified as a prohibited Class A drug under the rules of the International Federation for Equestrian Sports (FEI) and is similarly restricted or banned by many other equestrian organizations. The drug can be detected in the blood for 2 to 3 days and in the urine for up to 15 days following administration. Flunixin should not be combined with other NSAIDs or corticosteroids, as this increases the risk of gastric ulcers, right dorsal colitis, and kidney disease. Veterinarians should also exercise caution when combining flunixin with anticoagulants or aminoglycoside antibiotics. To protect the gastrointestinal tract, flunixin is often used in conjunction with medications such as omeprazole, sucralfate, or cimetidine. Flunixin can be administered orally as a paste or granules mixed with feed. It can also be given intramuscularly or intravenously. However, due to its irritant properties, the intravenous route is preferred, and in cattle, this is the labeled route of administration. Dosages are typically reduced for ponies, which are more susceptible to NSAID-related side effects, as well as for horses with compromised liver or kidney function, such as older animals. In the United States, flunixin is sold under trade names such as Banamine, Flunixamine, Citation, Equileve, and Meflosyl Solution. In the United Kingdom, it is marketed as Flunixin (licensed by Norbrook), Finadyne, and Cronyxin. In South Africa and Australia, Finadyne is a common trade name. In India, it is marketed as Megludyne by Virbac (veterinary).
